newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. warns Afghan Taleban on suppressing women.
newsitem.headline: U.N. warns Afghan Taleban on suppressing women.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Monday warned the radical Islamic militia Taleban that discrimination against women in employment and education would could seriously affect relief programmes.
In a statement, he also told U.N. agencies to adhere to the U.N. Charter on equal rights for women and speak with one voice in Afghanistan.
"We have decided to restate our single, system-wide policy on the question of gender equality," he said in a statement sent to the many U.N. agencies operating in Afghanistan.
He said that the agencies had to respect any requirements from donors as well as recipients providing they "do not conflict with our stated principles."

Restrictions reported to date, such as denying women employment and education, could "have serious repercussions on the ability of the United Nations to deliver programmes of relief and reconstruction," he warned.

The United Nations, he said, wanted to cooperate with local authorities "but at the same time, the U.N. system is obliged to be guided by the norms and requirements stated in the (U.N.) Charter," he added.
His chief spokeswoman, Sylvana Foa, told reporters, "The U.N.'s Koran says there has to be equality between the sexes."
"The idea is to send a message that this is the way the U.N. operates and that we have our set of rules just the way they do," she said.
For example, agencies like the World Food Programme needed to hire local women to help with food distribution. In Kabul along more than 25,000 widows are dependend on food aid.

"We want to be able to go directly to the women, go to their homes, have them collect the food and women have to talk to women in their own language," Foa said. Another programme rewarded women with cooking oil if they showed up for pre-natal care.

With the Taleban having captured the capital of Kabul last month, women, many of them war widows, were forbidden to work or attend school or university. Some were beaten on the streets for not being shrouded from head to toe.

Some U.N. programmes have already been suspended because Afghan women aid workers have been forced to stay home. After protests from Afghan women's groups and others, UNICEF last year stopped school education programmes in some Taleban areas because girls have been expelled.

Many Taleban leaders have said that the strict rules would change and be reviewed in the future but U.N. sources said that in most of the provincial areas under Taleban control this was not the case despite similar promises last year.

The United Nations also has a political mission in Afghanistan led by Norbert Holl of Germany. According to U.N. Assistant Secretary Rosario Green, a woman will assume one of the vacant posts on the mission if the group continues functioning in Afghanistan.
